description: In 1429, a 17-year-old peasant girl persuaded the Dauphin to hand her an army. Within months, Joan of Arc turned around a war France seemed to have lost.

hero.hook: Seventeen years old, one banner, and a kingdom that tips over.

blocks.text: In **1429**, France looked lost. The English and their Burgundian allies held the north. The Dauphin Charles, heir to the throne, was stuck south of the Loire. Then a **17-year-old** peasant girl from Domrémy in Lorraine said she had a mission from God.

**Joan of Arc** did not only change the front line. She changed who could claim to be the rightful king. In her day many people believed in [[providentialism]], the idea that God steps directly into history. Joan said she knew which of the two claimants He had chosen.

The Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) set the kings of England (the Plantagenets) against the kings of France (the Valois). By 1429 the country was also torn by a civil war: the [[Armagnacs]], loyal to the Dauphin, against the [[Burgundians]], allies of the English. The [[Treaty of Troyes (1420)]] had disinherited the Dauphin in favor of the King of England. In Paris, Henry VI was proclaimed king. Charles VII was no more than the “little king of Bourges.”

blocks.caption: Joan of Arc, the face of the French reconquest

blocks.text: In **1428**, the English laid siege to **Orléans**, a key city on the Loire. If it fell, the south lay open. It was in that despair that Joan left Lorraine.
Joan never killed an enemy with her own hand. She preferred to carry her banner rather than a sword, so she could lead without shedding blood herself.

Born around **1412**, Joan said she heard Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret from the age of **13**. Their order: lift the siege of Orléans, then take the Dauphin to the [[coronation at Reims]]. Only that rite, anointing with holy oil in Reims cathedral, made a true king in the eyes of the kingdom.

In **February 1429**, at **Chinon** on the Loire, she picked Charles out from a crowd of courtiers in disguise. The theologians of Poitiers questioned her for three weeks, then cleared her. She was given armor, a banner, and a convoy for Orléans.
At Poitiers, matrons checked that she was a virgin. People believed a witch could not be one, since she would have made a carnal pact with the devil.

In **May 1429**, Joan broke a seven-month siege in **nine days**. The French troops came alive. The English fell back. On **July 17**, Charles was crowned at Reims, deep inside Burgundian territory. The Treaty of Troyes was politically dead: the king had been anointed.

Then the momentum ran out. Paris held. On **May 23, 1430**, at Compiègne, Joan was captured by the Burgundians, then sold to the English for **10,000 livres**. In Rouen, Bishop [[Pierre Cauchon]], a supporter of the English, staged a trial for heresy. On **May 30, 1431**, she was burned alive.

events.detail: A French victory, and the effective end of the war.
events.title: Castillon

blocks.text: Joan's death did not stop the reconquest. She had welded national feeling to the throne. In **1456**, Charles VII had her rehabilitated. The war ended at [[Castillon]], in Guyenne, in **1453**, with the English almost entirely driven out of France.
Illiterate peasant, war leader, martyr, saint: Joan crosses the centuries as a figure every age reinvents. In a few months she made possible what had looked lost.

In **1429**, Joan of Arc, aged **17**, lifted the siege of Orléans and had Charles VII crowned. Burned in **1431** and rehabilitated in **1456**, she remains the symbol of a kingdom that refused to disappear.
